title: The Story of Saint Rafqa
summary: A girl from Himlaya becomes a sister who teaches, protects a child, and learns to receive care in illness.
coverAlt: Painterly illustration of young Boutroussieh with her mother in a Lebanese hillside village

pages.title: A Little Girl in Himlaya
pages.body: In 1832, in the mountain village of Himlaya in Lebanon, a baby girl was born. She was baptized Boutroussieh, and she was the only child of her parents. Her mother's name was Rafqa. Remember that name, because it comes back later in our story. Her mother and father taught her to love God and to pray every day. But when Boutroussieh was only seven years old, her mother died. It was the first great sadness of her life, and it was not the last.

pages.title: Her Own Choice
pages.body: When Boutroussieh's father had money troubles, she went to live and work in another family's home for four years. When she grew older, her family hoped she would marry. But Boutroussieh felt drawn to give her life to God. She walked to the convent of Our Lady of Deliverance in Bikfaya, with two girls she met along the road. She stepped into the church and looked up at the icon of Mary. She felt a deep joy, and she felt that God was telling her yes.

pages.title: Bread and Letters
pages.body: Boutroussieh became a sister, and she was sent to the seminary in Ghazir. There she took charge of the kitchen. Imagine the work of a seminary kitchen: bread, soup, and a lot of dishes. In her free time she studied Arabic, handwriting, and numbers, and she helped girls who wanted to learn. Some days she was cooking, and some days she was reading, and in every moment she was serving. Sister Boutroussieh was learning to love God and her neighbors with her hands.

pages.title: The Child Under Her Robe
pages.body: One day the sisters sent her to teach the faith to children in Deir el-Kamar. Those were frightening years in Lebanon. There was fighting in the streets. The Church's account says that, once, Rafqa hid a child under her robe and kept the child safe. She was afraid, but she did not let fear decide. Later, in the village of Maad, she and another sister spent seven years building a school for girls who had nowhere to learn.

pages.title: A New Home and a New Name
pages.body: After a hard time in her community, Boutroussieh needed to decide where God was calling her next. She prayed in a church dedicated to Saint George, and she told people about a dream. In the dream, three saints told her to join the Lebanese Maronite Order. So in 1871, she walked to the monastery of Saint Simon in Aito. The sisters welcomed her. She received a new name, Rafqa, which was the name of the mother she had lost. Now the name had come back.

pages.title: Care in a Time of Pain
pages.body: Years later, a terrible pain began in her head and her eyes. The Church's account says that she had prayed to share in the suffering of Jesus. That was her own private prayer, and it is not a prayer for children. Pain is never something a child should ask for. When you hurt, you tell a grown-up and you get help. Her superior did that for her. She made sure Rafqa saw a doctor, but Rafqa lost the sight in one eye.

pages.title: Hands That Still Worked
pages.body: In 1897, six sisters moved to a new monastery, Saint Joseph in Jrabta, and Rafqa went with them. In 1899 she lost the sight in her other eye. Her body grew weaker, and many things became hard. But her hands could still work. She used them to knit socks and make clothing for others. The sisters took care of her, and she gave back what she could. It is good to be helped. It is good to help. In Rafqa's life, both happened every day.

pages.title: A Saint for Lebanon
pages.body: Rafqa died on the twenty-third of March, 1914, at the monastery in Jrabta. She was buried there. Years later, the Church studied her life with care. In 1985 she was declared blessed. In 2001, Pope John Paul II declared her a saint. People still travel to Jrabta to pray, and to say thank you. She did not have a perfect life. But she had a life where love kept showing up.

pages.title: What She Left Behind
pages.body: What would you carry from Rafqa's life? You might remember the girl who walked to the convent because she knew her heart. Or the sister who hid a child under her robe. Or the teacher who built a school, or the nun who kept knitting socks when her world had grown very small. She showed that you do not need to do everything. You can notice one person, and offer one kind of help that is truly useful.

pages.title: Points of reflection
pages.body:
Here is something to wonder about. Rafqa cooked, taught, and knitted, and she gave all of it to God. What ordinary thing could you offer to God this week?

Would you like to read what Jesus said about helping others? It is in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-five, verse forty: "Whatever you did for one of these least brothers of mine, you did for me."

This week, try one small kind step. Ask a trusted grown-up how you could help someone who is sick or lonely, and do it together. And if you are hurting, tell someone safe. Asking for help is a brave way to take care of yourself.

A little prayer: Jesus, thank you for Saint Rafqa, who loved you in her work and in her pain. Help me to notice people who need me. Help me to ask for help when I need it, too. Amen.
